clinicalPearls: PH is diagnosed when mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) is >20 mmHg by right heart catheterisation; this threshold was lowered from the older >=25 mmHg cut-off to emphasise earlier disease detection (p.2185, 2191).
The most common causes of PH are left heart disease or primary lung disease; pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is an uncommon but distinct subtype with an obliterative arteriopathy (p.2185).
Most patients present with dyspnoea and/or fatigue; oedema, chest pain, presyncope and syncope are less common and signal more advanced disease (p.2188).

The current WSPH classification (last revised 2018, Sixth World Symposium) defines five groups: 1 = PAH; 2 = PH due to left heart disease; 3 = PH due to chronic lung disease/hypoxia or sleep-disordered breathing; 4 = chronic thromboembolic PH (CTEPH); 5 = miscellaneous/multifactorial (p.2191).

Echocardiography with agitated-saline (bubble) study is the most important initial screening test; estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure >35 mmHg, a notched continuous-wave Doppler waveform, or a hypertrophied/dilated right ventricle supports the diagnosis (p.2188).

Hemodynamic subtypes by RHC: precapillary PH = PAWP/LVEDP <=15 mmHg with PVR >2.0 Wood units; isolated postcapillary PH = PAWP >15 mmHg with PVR <=2.0 WU; combined pre-/postcapillary PH = mPAP >20 mmHg with PAWP >15 mmHg and PVR >2.0 WU (p.2191).
In PAH, an isolated reduction in diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) on pulmonary function testing is a classic finding (p.2189).

BNP and NT-proBNP correlate with right ventricular dysfunction, hemodynamic severity and functional status in PAH, and NT-proBNP can serve as a biomarker of treatment response once a baseline is established (p.2191).

Vasoreactivity testing (with short-acting agents such as inhaled nitric oxide or inhaled epoprostenol) is reserved for idiopathic or hereditary PAH; a positive response is a fall in mPAP by >=10 mmHg to an absolute level <=40 mmHg without a fall in cardiac output, seen in <5% of patients but carrying a particularly favourable prognosis (p.2191).

CTEPH is curable in many patients by surgical pulmonary endarterectomy but is widely underdiagnosed; ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scanning remains the primary screening test and should be considered in any PH of unclear cause (p.2190-2191).
harrison.pathophysiology: PAH arises from apoptosis resistance, cell proliferation, dysregulated metabolism and increased oxidant stress in pulmonary vascular cells, pericytes and adventitial fibroblasts, producing hypertrophic, fibrotic and plexogenic remodelling of distal (small) pulmonary arterioles with extracellular-matrix expansion, reduced vascular compliance and in-situ thrombosis. This raises pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) and mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP). To preserve cardiac output against the elevated right-ventricular afterload, RV work increases; sustained overload depletes myocardial energy and causes right ventricular-pulmonary arterial uncoupling, and in end-stage disease cardiac output and mPAP both fall. The most common germline driver of hereditary PAH is a BMPR2 variant (a TGF-beta superfamily receptor) with variable penetrance (as low as ~20%); other drivers include TBX4 and SOX17, and EIF2AK4 for pulmonary veno-occlusive disease. In group 2 PH the hallmark is elevated left atrial pressure causing pulmonary venous hypertension, venule sclerosis and secondary arteriolar remodelling. (p.2185-2192)
additionalDifferentials: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)
Connective tissue disease, especially systemic sclerosis-associated PAH
Congenital heart disease with intracardiac shunt / Eisenmenger's syndrome
Hepatopulmonary syndrome (distinct: causes intrapulmonary shunting, not pulmonary vascular remodelling)
infectionMimics: HIV infection (HIV-PAH is an important cause of mortality in HIV-infected patients)
Schistosomiasis (affects >230 million worldwide, ~5% develop PAH; among the most common causes of PAH globally)
nonInfectiousMimics: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
additionalInvestigations: Right heart catheterisation (RHC) - gold standard for diagnosis and severity assessment; required mPAP >20 mmHg
Transthoracic echocardiography with agitated-saline (bubble) study - most important initial screening test
Electrocardiography - may show right ventricular hypertrophy or strain in advanced disease
Chest roentgenography - enlargement of central pulmonary arteries and obliteration of the retrosternal space
Pulmonary function testing including DLCO (isolated low DLCO classic for PAH)
High-resolution CT of the chest (vascular pruning, distinguishing ILD/emphysema/overlap; signs of venous congestion)
Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan - primary screen for CTEPH
CT pulmonary angiography and digital subtraction pulmonary angiography (definitive for CTEPH; shows webbing, stricture, tapering)
6-minute walk distance (6-MWD) for functional capacity and prognosis
Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET); peak VO2 <15 mL/kg/min is prognostic but not diagnostic
Nocturnal oximetry screening in all patients (nocturnal desaturation common even without sleep-disordered breathing)
Serology: HIV test (when indicated), antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, anti-Scl-70; liver function and hepatitis serology; methamphetamine screening where relevant
redFlags: Signs of right ventricular failure: elevated jugular venous pressure, lower-extremity oedema, ascites
Rapid progression of symptoms with severely reduced exercise capacity
Decompensated right heart failure (the major cause of mortality if untreated)
Significant decline in exercise tolerance from baseline even when CPET appears reassuring (e.g. in athletes - may indicate early PAH or subacute PE)
harrison.prognosis: If left untreated, PH carries a high mortality rate, largely owing to decompensated right heart failure. Idiopathic PAH is progressive and leads to right heart failure and early mortality; in left-sided heart failure or HFpEF even mildly elevated mPAP carries adverse outcome. Among IPAH, prevalence favours women ~3:1 but hemodynamics are more severe and prognosis less favourable in men. Hereditary BMPR2 PAH presents younger with more severe hemodynamics and greater clinical risk (conversion ~2.3%/year in carriers). Vasoreactive responders (<5%) have a particularly favourable prognosis. Scleroderma-associated PAH and HIV-PAH carry especially poor prognoses; portopulmonary hypertension is a marker of adverse post-liver-transplant outcome (up to 100% mortality reported with mPAP >=50 mmHg in one study). Peak VO2 <15 mL/kg/min is prognostic. (p.2185, 2191-2192)
pitfalls: Right heart catheterisation - not echocardiography - is the diagnostic gold standard; echocardiography only screens, and an echo in which tricuspid regurgitation is simply not detected does NOT exclude PH (PH is found in one-third of such patients).
PH symptoms are nonspecific, insidious and overlap with asthma, HFpEF and deconditioning, so the diagnosis is frequently missed without a reasonable index of suspicion.
Do not assume that PH in patients with comorbid cardiopulmonary disease (e.g. ILD, mitral valve disease) is merely an extension of the underlying condition rather than a specific entity.
Patients with left heart disease aggressively diuresed before RHC may falsely appear to have an isolated precapillary (PAH-like) profile - diuresis can mask the true hemodynamic classification.
A low peak VO2 occurs across the heart-lung disease spectrum and is NOT diagnostic of PH per se.

Chronic thromboembolic disease (thrombotic remodelling with reduced exercise capacity but without PH) requires consideration in patients with prior PE and dyspnoea even when echocardiography is reassuring.
harrison.severityClassification: World Symposium on Pulmonary Hypertension (WSPH) clinical classification (revised 2018) into 5 groups: Group 1 - pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH: idiopathic, heritable, drug/toxin-associated, or associated with connective tissue disease, HIV, portal hypertension, congenital heart disease, schistosomiasis; plus PVOD/PCH and persistent PH of the newborn); Group 2 - PH associated with left heart disease (HFpEF, HFrEF, valvular, congenital/acquired postcapillary); Group 3 - PH associated with lung disease and/or hypoxia (obstructive, restrictive, mixed, hypoventilation, high-altitude hypoxia, developmental); Group 4 - PH associated with pulmonary artery obstruction (CTEPH and other obstructions); Group 5 - PH with unclear/multifactorial mechanisms (haematological, systemic, metabolic, chronic renal failure +/- haemodialysis, pulmonary tumour thrombotic microangiopathy, fibrosing mediastinitis). Hemodynamic categorisation by RHC: precapillary, isolated postcapillary, and combined pre-/postcapillary PH. (Table 294-1, p.2191)
management: Classify by WHO group at a specialist centre, since treatment is group-specific and targeted PAH drugs can be harmful in left heart and lung disease

For Group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension, use targeted therapy with endothelin receptor antagonists, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors or guanylate cyclase stimulators and prostacyclin pathway agents, reserving calcium channel blockers for vasoreactive responders
For Group 2, optimise the underlying left heart disease rather than giving PAH-specific drugs
For Group 3, treat the underlying lung disease and hypoxaemia with long-term oxygen and address sleep-disordered breathing
For Group 4 chronic thromboembolic disease, provide lifelong anticoagulation with pulmonary endarterectomy, balloon pulmonary angioplasty or riociguat
Supportive care with diuretics for right heart failure, oxygen for hypoxaemia and pulmonary rehabilitation

Risk-stratify and reassess serially to guide escalation, refer to a specialist centre, and consider transplantation for refractory disease, with genetic counselling for heritable PAH such as BMPR2 variants
